title: The Centroid of a Tree

concept.title: A centroid is a node whose removal leaves no component bigger than half of the tree
body: If you remove a node from a tree, the rest falls apart into several components (one per neighbour). A **centroid** is a node for which the **largest** remaining component has at most `n / 2` nodes: it splits the tree into balanced parts. Every tree has one or two centroids (two only when the tree has an even number of nodes and an edge cuts it into two halves of `n / 2`). Centroids are the basis of divide and conquer on trees: cut at the centroid, and every piece is at most half as big, so there are only O(log n) levels.

To test a node `v`, root the tree anywhere and compute `size[v]`, the number of nodes in the subtree of `v`. The components after removing `v` are the subtrees of its children (sizes `size[c]`) and the "rest of the tree" above it, of size `n - size[v]`. So

body.code:
biggest[v] = max(n - size[v], max over children c of size[c])
v is a centroid  <=>  2 * biggest[v] <= n

body: The sizes are computed without recursion: list the nodes in breadth-first order and walk the list backwards, adding every node's size to its parent. While doing this, keep for every node the largest child size. The tree can be a path of 20000 nodes, so recursion is not an option. Print the centroids in increasing order.

statement: A tree with `m + 1` nodes is given by its `m` edges. A centroid is a node such that after its removal every remaining component has at most half of all the nodes (more precisely, at most `n / 2`, where `n = m + 1`, so twice the size of every component is at most `n`). Print all the centroids in increasing order, separated by spaces (there are one or two).
inputFormat: The first line has `m`, the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
outputFormat: The centroids in increasing order on one line.
constraints: The nodes are numbered 1 to m + 1, and the edges form a tree.
The tree can be a long path.

examples.note: Removing node 3 leaves the components {1, 2}, {4} and {5, 6}, all of size at most 3 = 6 / 2. Node 1 leaves {2} and {3, 4, 5, 6}: 4 > 3, so it is not a centroid. The only centroid is 3.

hints: Root the tree at node 1 and compute the subtree sizes from the breadth-first order, walked backwards.
The components after removing v are the child subtrees and the rest above v, of size n - size[v].
v is a centroid when twice the largest of these sizes is at most n.

explanation: With subtree sizes from a breadth-first order walked backwards, the largest component after removing v is the larger of n - size[v] and the biggest child subtree; v is a centroid when twice that is at most n.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

m = int(input())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

n = m + 1
adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)
parent = [0] * (n + 1)
parent[1] = -1
order = [1]
for v in order:
    for w in adj[v]:
        if w != parent[v]:
            parent[w] = v
            order.append(w)
size = [1] * (n + 1)
biggest_child = [0] * (n + 1)
for v in reversed(order[1:]):
    p = parent[v]
    size[p] += size[v]
    biggest_child[p] = max(biggest_child[p], size[v])
centroids = [v for v in range(1, n + 1) if 2 * max(n - size[v], biggest_child[v]) <= n]
print(*centroids)
